TOP NEWS " Heat stroke is suspected among 6 found dead in a shipping container at a rail yard near Texas border" via AP - A South Texas medical examiner believes heat stroke may have led to the death of six people thought to be immigrants who were found Sunday afternoon inside a shipping container at a Union Pacific rail yard near the Mexico border in Laredo, Texas. The people were found Sunday as workers were inspecting one of the containers, said Jose Baeza, a spokesperson for the Laredo Police Department. Police and fire crews arrived at the scene shortly afterward. They confirmed that there were six people dead, five men and one woman, Baeza told reporters. Dr. Corinne Stern , the Webb County Medical Examiner, is conducting autopsies and completed one for a 29-year-old Mexican woman who died of hyperthermia, or heat stroke. "I've ruled that an accidental death," she said. "I believe that the remaining individuals probably all succumbed to heat stroke as well, but their exams are not completed at this time, so I will not rule on their cause and manner yet." Stern found identification cards and cellphones that indicate the deceased may be from Mexico and Honduras, but fingerprints were taken and shared with U.S. Border Patrol to help confirm their identities and nationalities through the Missing Alien Program. The medical examiner's office also contacted the Mexican consulate after identifying the woman. "This was a horrific scene," Stern added, also noting that immigrant deaths is a common occurrence in the ten-county region her office covers. "This spring has been busier than it was this time last year," the medical examiner said. () " In parched Texas, a state fund to boost water projects falls almost $3 billion short of demand" via Colleen DeGuzman - As Texas struggles to meet the needs of a rapidly growing population, a state fund had $1.28 billion available this year to support projects that could deliver water even in a severe drought. Unfortunately, 23 worthy projects requested a total of $4.2 billion, prompting the state to deny 13 of them -- the first time the SWIFT fund had to say no to an applicant in its 11-year history. It was lamentable timing for a state plagued by a brutal drought and aging water infrastructure. "We have more demand than we actually have the capacity to fulfill this year," said Marvin Cole-Chaney , director of program administration and reporting for the Texas Water Development Board, which administers SWIFT, the State Water Implementation Fund for Texas. () " Gas power leapfrogs wind for first time in 10 years in Texas' grid connection queue" via Brandon Mulder and Chris Essig - A decade ago, wind power was surging in popularity and attracting huge investments that made Texas a national leader in renewable energy. But today, gas generation is making a big comeback, driven by a wave of data centers flooding into the state. For the last six months, the volume of gas generation in the Texas grid's interconnection queue -- the yearslong waiting list for electric generators wanting to connect to the grid -- has surpassed wind. It's the first time since January 2016 that gas has overtaken wind in the queue, a shift that reflects the policy and economic headwinds facing the wind industry and data centers favoring gas power as they seek to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom. "The data center explosion and their desire for 24/7 power probably excited a lot of gas developers, and that gas queue got bigger," said University of Texas professor of energy regulation David Spence. Like every power grid operator in the U.S., the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, uses the interconnection queue to manage and plan for new power generation coming online. But not all projects in the queue ultimately reach completion. According to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, or LBNL, only 22% of projects in ERCOT's queue actually get built, which is still the highest percentage of any grid in the nation. () " New Texas A&M president confirmed as university seeks stability" via AP - Regents on Wednesday unanimously appointed Susan Ballabina as president of Texas A&M, putting her in charge of the state's largest public university as it continues to deal with the fallout from its last president's resignation. Ballabina, who assumes the role on May 11, most recently served as executive vice chancellor for the Texas A&M University System, overseeing day-to-day operations across its 12 universities and eight state agencies. Prior to that, she was former Texas A&M President Mark A. Welsh III's chief of staff. Regents named Ballabina the sole finalist April 13. State law required them to wait 21 days before finalizing the hire. She initially served on the presidential search committee before recusing herself to apply for the job. "I was a reluctant applicant. I wasn't sure that this was something I wanted to do, but after going through the process and preparing for the various interviews, I got more and more excited," Ballabina said during the regents' meeting after their vote. The decision follows months of upheaval at the flagship campus after Welsh resigned amid political backlash over that was posted online. The search unfolded as regents took a more assertive role in responding to controversy and shaping what can be taught, part of a broader political remaking of Texas colleges under new state laws. () 2026 " Abbott's senior adviser warns Republicans not to let Texas flip" via Rachel Royster -** A senior adviser to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott warned two Tarrant County Republican clubs Wednesday of the possibility of Texas flipping if the party doesn't act. The same goes for Tarrant County, said Abbott's adviser and policy director, Steve Munisteri. Munisteri spoke to Tarrant Star Republican Women over lunch and the Cowtown Republican Women on Wednesday evening to discuss Texas' political landscape and what's at stake for Republicans () " How billionaires are helping Democrat James Talarico in the U.S. Senate race" via C. Moritz - James Talarico , a Texas Democratic primary candidate for U.S. Senate, frequently criticizes the influence of billionaires in politics and notably does not accept money from corporate political action committees. However, this does not preclude PACs and billionaires from promoting his campaign. Lone Star Rising, a super PAC created to support Talarico, has raised approximately $9 million from politically active billionaires and millionaires, with nearly half sourced from a dark money group that does not disclose its donors. Talarico has expressed support for banning super PACs and distances himself from Lone Star Rising, noting that federal law prohibits him from coordinating with the PAC or controlling its fundraising and spending. "Legally, I cannot do anything about what any super PAC does, whether supporting me or not supporting me," Talarico told reporters. "We've got super PACs on all sides. We've got super PACs in the middle that are playing on both sides. It's nothing that we have control over." () STATE GOVERNMENT " Texas reaches deal with youth camps over fiber‐optic rule tied to safety law" via Jack Fink - The Texas Department of State Health Services has struck a deal with youth camps over a requirement that they install a fiber‐optic internet connection to operate this summer. A group of camps filed suit against the state last month after the mandate was included in a camp safety law approved by lawmakers last year. The agreement stays the court proceedings until March 1, 2027. The legislation followed horrific flooding in Central Texas on July 4 that resulted in 25 campers and two counselors losing their lives at Camp Mystic. The camp's executive director also died. Under the agreement, camps that maintain redundant internet service and comply with all other safety requirements will not have their licenses denied if they have not installed fiber‐optic service. The agency said alternative broadband options - including cellular, microwave, or satellite - are acceptable as long as they meet the definition of broadband under the Texas Government Code. On Tuesday, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and House Speaker Dustin Burrows , R‐Lubbock, issued a joint statement aimed at giving camps more flexibility. They acknowledged that some camps were struggling to comply and that other forms of reliable redundant internet access exist. () " Texas prisons saw 2,500% increase in overdose deaths in 7 years, TDCJ leader says" via Toluwani Osibamowo - Overdose deaths in Texas prisons jumped 2,480% over the past seven years, a state prison official told lawmakers this week as they consider ways to curb contraband in Texas correctional facilities. There were 129 recorded overdose deaths among people in Texas Department of Criminal Justice custody last year, said Bobby Lumpkin , TDCJ's executive director. That's up from five such deaths in 2018. The data was presented to senators Monday but has not been made publicly available online. It represents a relatively small portion of the 142,000 people Lumpkin said are currently in TDCJ custody. "The root cause is a dependency and an addiction to that type of illicit substances," he told lawmakers during a Senate Committee on Criminal Justice hearing. "It unfortunately is an extension of the criminal element that even though they've been through the judicial system, been sentenced, they still depend back on that type of activity." () " TEA selects Connally schools superintendent to lead takeover" via Sneha Dey - In a takeover of Connally ISD, the state brought in an educator from a neighboring Waco district to accelerate academic gains. Texas Education Agency Commissioner Mike Morath picked Josie Gutierrez to lead the 2,000-student district, citing her success in improving outcomes and strengthening teacher retention as deputy superintendent and an assistant superintendent of human resources for Waco ISD. Gutierrez is the latest superintendent Morath has appointed in recent weeks to helm districts after the commissioner took control from locally elected school trustees over poor academic performance. Other state interventions include those in Fort Worth, Lake Worth and Beaumont. () " AG Ken Paxton leaves Odessa hanging after tax investigation" via Carlos Nogueras Ramos - Last October was like any other for most Odessa city employees. Parks employees unveiled a new sign. The police department gave a tour to homeschooled kids. A council member attended a fundraising event for culinary students. But amid everyday responsibilities, top local officials were scrambling to respond to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton 's demand that they justify a recently approved tax rate hike. The state had just passed a law that prohibited cities from raising taxes without completing financial audits. Paxton had singled out four cities, and Odessa was among them. "To uphold my duty as the Attorney General to ensure that municipalities are following audit laws, I am formally launching an investigation into the City of Odessa to determine whether the new tax rate is illegal," Paxton wrote. "Furthermore, I am demanding that the new tax rate not be implemented until I complete my investigation." City officials moved quickly, gathering hundreds of pages of documents, including minutes from relevant City Council meetings and evidence that the tax rate was published in a newspaper. By December 2025, Odessa had handed over the documents Paxton requested. () LOCAL GOVERNMENT " Former Mayor Mike Rawlings launches campaign to relocate Dallas City Hall, revive downtown" via Devyani Chhetri - Mike Rawlings is ramping up the fight over City Hall as questions grow over how to reshape downtown Dallas. Rawlings launched a coordinated campaign Thursday to build support for relocating City Hall, using newspaper and social media ads, a website and other outreach to promote redevelopment there, possibly for a sports arena and entertainment district. In an interview with The Dallas Morning News, Rawlings said his efforts are designed to shift the City Council beyond wrangling over repair estimates and focus instead on how best to use the site as a catalyst to attract new business and reinvigorate its southern edge. "My fear about downtown is we're thinking too small," he said. "We've got to have a force to change this." The campaign marks an escalation in the increasingly high-stakes fight over City Hall's future. It's been a clash of competing visions, centered on whether the council should invest in costly updates to the building or move government operations and pursue a different use for that large swath of land as the Dallas Mavericks look for a new home. The council is expected to make that consequential choice in June after city staffers present a cost comparison of staying or leaving. Previous votes have indicated the mayor and eight council members support exploring relocation, while six members are opposed. () " Mayor John Whitmire's new city budget shrinks Houston's future deficits" via Church - Finance projections at Houston City Hall show steps city officials took to close a budget deficit in the proposal Mayor John Whitmire announced Tuesday would significantly reduce future red ink. Whitmire's proposed $7.5 billion budget includes a new $5 monthly fee on city trash customers to help the city's troubled Solid Waste Management Department, which has long struggled to pick up trash, recycling and yard waste on time. That fee would generate $24 million in new revenue -- a rare step at City Hall. But the proposal would also change the structure of the city budget by moving the $117 million solid waste budget out of the strained general fund and into Houston Public Works, within the city utility system. The mayor also proposes charging the utility system $104 million - or 5% of its annual gross revenues - for its pipes using the city right of way, money that also would flow into the general fund. () " Corpus Christi City Council votes to start talks on building a new desalination plant" via -- As Corpus Christi's water crisis looms and city leaders scramble for solutions, the City Council has voted 6-2 to move forward with talks for a new company to build a desalination plant. Houston-based AXE H2O is a two-month old company that says it can build a plant that can produce 150 million gallons of drinking water per day using natural gas, according to a report from The Texas Tribune. The city would pay $6.50 for 1,000 gallons of water. According to John Olson , the company's chairman, the project would be a private venture and construction would take about two years. The company estimates it would cost about $1.3 billion to build. Council members Roland Barrera and Cynthia Campos -- who made up the two votes against the project -- were skeptical, with Campos saying it sounded "too good to be true." () " FBI says 6th Street shooter acted alone in March 1 mass shooting" via Dalton Huey - The FBI said Thursday that its investigation into the March 1 mass shooting in downtown Austin found no evidence that the gunman was directed by a foreign terrorist organization. The press release notes that investigators learned that the perpetrator, Ndiaga Diagne , had expressed admiration for former Iranian AyatollahAli Khamenei and held grievances over American and Israeli attacks against Iran. The FBI also stated that Diagne, a 53-year-old Senegal-born man and naturalized U.S. citizen as of 2013, had legally purchased a handgun in August 2017 and a rifle in October 2017. Diagne used both of those guns in his attack on West Sixth Street, in which he killed three people and injured 15 others. Responding Austin police officers confronted and killed him minutes after he opened fire. The three killed in the shooting were Savitha Shan , Ryder Harrington and Jorge Pederson. In the initial aftermath of the attack, FBI officials said that there were "indicators" that it was an act of terrorism. The FBI said Thursday that its investigation determined Diagne acted alone and had not received outside funding, operational support or direction for the attack. He also had not been the subject of any prior FBI investigation, according to the press release. Investigators also said Diagne's "violent behavior" escalated due to "specific personal triggers and grievances" connected to the Iran war. The FBI found Diagne admired Khamenei, who had been killed in the U.S. and Israeli attacks one day before the shooting. () TRUMP ADMINISTRATION " EPA orders cleanup of toxic waste superfund site in San Jacinto River" via Rebekah F. Ward - Channelview-area leaders celebrated Wednesday after the Environmental Protection Agency ordered Waste Management and International Paper Co. to begin hauling toxic mud from a dioxin-filled waste pit that lurked in the San Jacinto River for decades. "It's a good day to be in Harris County," said Tom Ramsey , the county commissioner for the area surrounding the waste pits, as he called the San Jacinto River the "lifeblood" of the region. The cost estimate for cleanup of the underwater waste, known as the northern impoundment of the San Jacinto waste pits, has now climbed to a quarter of a billion dollars. The companies do not have a mandated excavation date yet, though they must respond to the federal government within 10 days of the April 28 order. According to federal Superfund law, they could owe three times the total cost of work if the EPA has to take over cleanup efforts. () BUSINESS NEWS " BlackRock invests $30M in Texas electrician training amidst data center boom" via Schwager -- Custom homebuilder Gene Lantrip has a slight problem. He's got a backload of about 15 houses right now, partially due to a recent boom of data centers in the region. "Oracle came in", he recalled "The next thing you know, they put out a call for 500 electricians"; Among those electricians were ones who helped put the finishing touches on the homes Lantrip builds. "Local guys right now in Abilene, starting out and make $15 an hour, the good ones make up for $25 an hour," Lantrip says. He says the data center companies are willing to pay double -- and he can't compete. "So our electricians, what they started doing was hiring inexperienced young kids and teaching them the trades -- on-the-job training," he said. "My electrician used to have a team of about 12 guys... Now they have one lead guy and about five young kids... When they had 12 guys, they can knock out three houses, but now it takes them all day to do one house." This comes at a time where the demand for Lantrip's services are as high as ever. "There's like 14,000 temporary workers out there working in right now, and they all need a place to stay," he said. BlackRock, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, faces similar problems. "As the largest investor in infrastructure, we hear in every project, 'We don't have enough workers. We can't find the workers. We're challenged. We're going to have delays," BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said. "When you have delays in your projects, that means it costs more money." () " Nvidia could bring thousands of jobs to Austin. Here's how." via Karoline Leonard - Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with a Disney robot during an Nvidia conference focusing on artificial intelligence in San Jose, Calif., on March 16. The artificial intelligence chipmaker announced a partnership with glassmaker Corning to build three new factories in North Carolina and Texas, creating more than 3,000 new jobs. The world's most valuable company might bring thousands of jobs to Austin as Nvidia ups its investment in Texas. Artificial intelligence chipmaker Nvidia Corp. and glassmaker Corning Inc. announced plans to build three new plants dedicated to manufacturing light and glass technologies for AI manufacturing in North Carolina and Texas. The companies, which both have significant business ties to the Austin area, promised to create more than 3,000 jobs at the factories. () " Is Brownsville getting a refinery? America First CEO is confident; industry analyst skeptical" via Steve Clark - When Donald Trump announced on Truth Social March 10 that Brownsville would be the site of the first U.S. oil refinery to be built in 50 years, it seemed to come out of the blue. But in fact, Port of Brownsville officials have been in communication with the principals behind the proposed America First Refining (AFR) project for about a dozen years, according to Brownsville Navigation District Chairman Steve Guerra. Back in June 2024, AFR founder and CEO John Calce announced that his company (then Element Fuel Holdings) had completed the site preparation and pre-construction work for a large oil refinery at the port. In a statement, he said the company had secured the permits necessary to construct and operate a refinery with a capacity of more than 160,000 BPD, or "approximately 6.7 million gallons, per day of finished gasoline, diesel and jet fuel." Reuters reported at the time that Calce had tried before to build a refinery at the port, through start-up firms ARX Energy and Jupiter Brownsville LLC, one such attempt resulting in a bankruptcy filing. * The **_Unhoused Persons Bill of Rights_** to end the unhoused crisis and support people without a safe place to live.

Requesting $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon this year, Trump said we need to spend money on war rather than healthcare or childcare.
He’s saying the quiet part out loud: no matter who’s president, our government always finds money for wars but not for working people.
I’m leading fights in Congress to move our tax dollars away from funding genocides and human rights abuses at home and abroad. Instead, our taxpayer dollars must fund communities’ needs.
I’m unafraid to fight for the bold and transformative changes that working families need. My recently introduced policies include:
* The **_Ban Warehouse Detention Act_****** to stop ICE warehouse detention centers.
* The **_Medicines for the People Act_** to establish a public option for developing and researching medicines. It would move our government to produce medications and devices, breaking up Big Pharma’s monopoly, lowering the cost of prescriptions and healthcare, and prioritizing life-saving innovations rather than corporate profits.

body:
Peter—

UPDATE: We expected a decision tonight in Louisiana v. FDA following the one-week stay that Justice Alito issued last week. We've just heard that the Supreme Court has extended the stay until Thursday at 5 PM EDT.

We know that Mifepristone is safe and effective, and for now it is still widely available. We will follow up with you later this week as we have more news.

Thank you for staying in the fight! [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]

Nancy

🚨 BREAKING NEWS FROM LOUISIANA 🚨
Dear Peter,
The fight to protect abortion access has just reached the Supreme Court. [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]
Peter—FIGHT BACK [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]
Last week, the Fifth Circuit sided with Louisiana and reinstated an outdated, medically unnecessary requirement that mifepristone be dispensed in person—threatening access by mail and at pharmacies nationwide. This morning, the Court temporarily agreed to stay the ruling until next Monday. But this fight is far from over.
Medication abortion accounts for more than 60% of abortions in the U.S. each year. Since Roe was overturned, telehealth abortion requests have doubled. For people in rural areas—hours from the nearest clinic—it was a lifeline.
PROTECT MIFE [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]
More than 7.5 million people have used it safely. Hundreds of studies back it. [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion] Restricting mifepristone is not about safety—it's about making abortion as difficult, expensive, and unreachable as possible.
DEFEND ABORTION CARE [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]
Extremists are stripping away reproductive freedom piece by piece: criminalizing care, intimidating doctors, and forcing patients to navigate a cruel maze of bans and restrictions. [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]
We refuse to accept it.
For decades, the Center for Reproductive Rights has been challenging coordinated attacks on your health care in courtrooms across the country, at every level. [https://secure.reproductiverights.org/a/support-medication-abortion]
This fight is no different. But stopping these attacks requires sustained legal action, and our ability to fight and win depends on people like you. Stay with us—we'll keep you updated as things unfold.In solidarity,

**" Heat stroke is suspected among 6 found dead in a shipping container at a rail yard near Texas border"** via AP**** - A South Texas medical examiner believes heat stroke may have led to the death of six people thought to be immigrants who were found Sunday afternoon inside a shipping container at a Union Pacific rail yard near the Mexico border in Laredo, Texas.

The people were found Sunday as workers were inspecting one of the containers, said Jose Baeza, a spokesperson for the Laredo Police Department.

Police and fire crews arrived at the scene shortly afterward. They confirmed that there were six people dead, five men and one woman, Baeza told reporters.

Dr. **Corinne Stern** , the Webb County Medical Examiner, is conducting autopsies and completed one for a 29-year-old Mexican woman who died of hyperthermia, or heat stroke. "I've ruled that an accidental death," she said. "I believe that the remaining individuals probably all succumbed to heat stroke as well, but their exams are not completed at this time, so I will not rule on their cause and manner yet."

Stern found identification cards and cellphones that indicate the deceased may be from Mexico and Honduras, but fingerprints were taken and shared with U.S. Border Patrol to help confirm their identities and nationalities through the Missing Alien Program.

The medical examiner's office also contacted the Mexican consulate after identifying the woman.

"This was a horrific scene," Stern added, also noting that immigrant deaths is a common occurrence in the ten-county region her office covers. "This spring has been busier than it was this time last year," the medical examiner said. (_[AP](https://substack.com/redirect/702b690a-7f63-4adf-b7f9-c848ac8a96ac?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_)

**" In parched Texas, a state fund to boost water projects falls almost $3 billion short of demand"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/e652dd37-9a63-4d73-bed1-17ddc199d8c4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Colleen DeGuzman** - As Texas struggles to meet the needs of a rapidly growing population, a state fund had $1.28 billion available this year to support projects that could deliver water even in a severe drought.

Unfortunately, 23 worthy projects requested a total of $4.2 billion, prompting the state to deny 13 of them -- the first time the SWIFT fund had to say no to an applicant in its 11-year history.

It was lamentable timing for a state plagued by a brutal drought and aging water infrastructure.

"We have more demand than we actually have the capacity to fulfill this year," said **Marvin Cole-Chaney** , director of program administration and reporting for the Texas Water Development Board, which administers SWIFT, the State Water Implementation Fund for Texas. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/e652dd37-9a63-4d73-bed1-17ddc199d8c4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Gas power leapfrogs wind for first time in 10 years in Texas' grid connection queue"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/13affc28-2c29-4a57-8702-c3e95a3562b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Brandon Mulder** and **Chris Essig** - A decade ago, wind power was surging in popularity and attracting huge investments that made Texas a national leader in renewable energy. But today, gas generation is making a big comeback, driven by a wave of data centers flooding into the state.

For the last six months, the volume of gas generation in the Texas grid's interconnection queue -- the yearslong waiting list for electric generators wanting to connect to the grid -- has surpassed wind. It's the first time since January 2016 that gas has overtaken wind in the queue, a shift that reflects the policy and economic headwinds facing the wind industry and data centers favoring gas power as they seek to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom.

"The data center explosion and their desire for 24/7 power probably excited a lot of gas developers, and that gas queue got bigger," said University of Texas professor of energy regulation **David Spence**.

Like every power grid operator in the U.S., the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, uses the interconnection queue to manage and plan for new power generation coming online. But not all projects in the queue ultimately reach completion. According to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, or LBNL, only 22% of projects in ERCOT's queue actually get built, which is still the highest percentage of any grid in the nation. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/13affc28-2c29-4a57-8702-c3e95a3562b0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" New Texas A&M president confirmed as university seeks stability"** via AP**** - Regents on Wednesday unanimously appointed Susan Ballabina as president of Texas A&M, putting her in charge of the state's largest public university as it continues to deal with the fallout from its last president's resignation.

Ballabina, who assumes the role on May 11, most recently served as executive vice chancellor for the Texas A&M University System, overseeing day-to-day operations across its 12 universities and eight state agencies. Prior to that, she was former Texas A&M President Mark A. Welsh III's chief of staff.

Regents named Ballabina the sole finalist April 13. State law required them to wait 21 days before finalizing the hire. She initially served on the presidential search committee before recusing herself to apply for the job.

"I was a reluctant applicant. I wasn't sure that this was something I wanted to do, but after going through the process and preparing for the various interviews, I got more and more excited," Ballabina said during the regents' meeting after their vote.

The decision follows months of upheaval at the flagship campus after Welsh resigned amid political backlash over [a secretly recorded classroom discussion of gender identity](https://substack.com/redirect/c3388dcd-80f0-4680-887d-8122e6241cfd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) that was posted online.

The search unfolded as regents took a more assertive role in responding to controversy and shaping what can be taught, part of a broader political remaking of Texas colleges under new state laws. (_[AP](https://substack.com/redirect/9fbdd4df-689b-4387-b2ef-87b7a6ec16cc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_)
* * *
**2026**
**" Abbott's senior adviser warns Republicans not to let Texas flip"** via [Fort Worth Star-Telegram](https://substack.com/redirect/1dcfab26-519d-48c6-b59a-b87dba63e9dc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Rachel Royster** -**** A senior adviser to Texas Gov. **Greg Abbott** warned two Tarrant County Republican clubs Wednesday of the possibility of Texas flipping if the party doesn't act.

The same goes for Tarrant County, said Abbott's adviser and policy director, **Steve Munisteri**.

Munisteri spoke to Tarrant Star Republican Women over lunch and the Cowtown Republican Women on Wednesday evening to discuss Texas' political landscape and what's at stake for Republicans _([FWST](https://substack.com/redirect/1dcfab26-519d-48c6-b59a-b87dba63e9dc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" How billionaires are helping Democrat James Talarico in the U.S. Senate race"** via [Austin American-Statesman](https://substack.com/redirect/4e99b810-8b1c-4d44-b91d-3d84e8a48072?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**John C. Moritz** - **James Talarico** , a Texas Democratic primary candidate for U.S. Senate, frequently criticizes the influence of billionaires in politics and notably does not accept money from corporate political action committees.

However, this does not preclude PACs and billionaires from promoting his campaign. Lone Star Rising, a super PAC created to support Talarico, has raised approximately $9 million from politically active billionaires and millionaires, with nearly half sourced from a dark money group that does not disclose its donors.

Talarico has expressed support for banning super PACs and distances himself from Lone Star Rising, noting that federal law prohibits him from coordinating with the PAC or controlling its fundraising and spending.

"Legally, I cannot do anything about what any super PAC does, whether supporting me or not supporting me," Talarico told reporters. "We've got super PACs on all sides. We've got super PACs in the middle that are playing on both sides. It's nothing that we have control over." _([AAS](https://substack.com/redirect/4e99b810-8b1c-4d44-b91d-3d84e8a48072?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_
* * *
**STATE GOVERNMENT**
**" Texas reaches deal with youth camps over fiber‐optic rule tied to safety law"** via [CBS News](https://substack.com/redirect/cf0d9ca8-4ce6-4a31-87a6-54f52a0fc460?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Jack Fink** - The Texas Department of State Health Services has struck a deal with youth camps over a requirement that they install a fiber‐optic internet connection to operate this summer. A group of camps filed suit against the state last month after the mandate was included in a camp safety law approved by lawmakers last year. The agreement stays the court proceedings until March 1, 2027.

The legislation followed horrific flooding in Central Texas on July 4 that resulted in 25 campers and two counselors losing their lives at Camp Mystic. The camp's executive director also died.

Under the agreement, camps that maintain redundant internet service and comply with all other safety requirements will not have their licenses denied if they have not installed fiber‐optic service. The agency said alternative broadband options - including cellular, microwave, or satellite - are acceptable as long as they meet the definition of broadband under the Texas Government Code.

On Tuesday, Lt. Gov. **Dan Patrick** and House Speaker **Dustin Burrows** , R‐Lubbock, issued a joint statement aimed at giving camps more flexibility. They acknowledged that some camps were struggling to comply and that other forms of reliable redundant internet access exist. _([CBS News](https://substack.com/redirect/cf0d9ca8-4ce6-4a31-87a6-54f52a0fc460?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Texas prisons saw 2,500% increase in overdose deaths in 7 years, TDCJ leader says"** via [KERA News](https://substack.com/redirect/5b475b6c-decb-4d83-bbb0-4e8592da05ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Toluwani Osibamowo** - Overdose deaths in Texas prisons jumped 2,480% over the past seven years, a state prison official told lawmakers this week as they consider ways to curb contraband in Texas correctional facilities.

There were 129 recorded overdose deaths among people in Texas Department of Criminal Justice custody last year, said **Bobby Lumpkin** , TDCJ's executive director. That's up from five such deaths in 2018.

The data was presented to senators Monday but has not been made publicly available online. It represents a relatively small portion of the 142,000 people Lumpkin said are currently in TDCJ custody.

"The root cause is a dependency and an addiction to that type of illicit substances," he told lawmakers during a Senate Committee on Criminal Justice hearing. "It unfortunately is an extension of the criminal element that even though they've been through the judicial system, been sentenced, they still depend back on that type of activity." _([KERA News](https://substack.com/redirect/5b475b6c-decb-4d83-bbb0-4e8592da05ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" TEA selects Connally schools superintendent to lead takeover"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/c975793c-8ff2-4aef-9e09-7d5068bd3309?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Sneha Dey** - In a takeover of Connally ISD, the state brought in an educator from a neighboring Waco district to accelerate academic gains.

Texas Education Agency Commissioner **Mike Morath** picked **Josie Gutierrez** to lead the 2,000-student district, citing her success in improving outcomes and strengthening teacher retention as deputy superintendent and an assistant superintendent of human resources for Waco ISD.

Gutierrez is the latest superintendent Morath has appointed in recent weeks to helm districts after the commissioner took control from locally elected school trustees over poor academic performance.

Other state interventions include those in Fort Worth, Lake Worth and Beaumont. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/c975793c-8ff2-4aef-9e09-7d5068bd3309?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" AG Ken Paxton leaves Odessa hanging after tax investigation"** via [The Texas Tribune](https://substack.com/redirect/5b646e7d-942c-463c-b402-5673e50eaab9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Carlos Nogueras Ramos** - Last October was like any other for most Odessa city employees. Parks employees unveiled a new sign. The police department gave a tour to homeschooled kids. A council member attended a fundraising event for culinary students.

But amid everyday responsibilities, top local officials were scrambling to respond to Texas Attorney General **Ken Paxton** 's demand that they justify a recently approved tax rate hike. The state had just passed a law that prohibited cities from raising taxes without completing financial audits. Paxton had singled out four cities, and Odessa was among them.

"To uphold my duty as the Attorney General to ensure that municipalities are following audit laws, I am formally launching an investigation into the City of Odessa to determine whether the new tax rate is illegal," Paxton wrote. "Furthermore, I am demanding that the new tax rate not be implemented until I complete my investigation."

City officials moved quickly, gathering hundreds of pages of documents, including minutes from relevant City Council meetings and evidence that the tax rate was published in a newspaper. By December 2025, Odessa had handed over the documents Paxton requested. _([TX TRIB](https://substack.com/redirect/5b646e7d-942c-463c-b402-5673e50eaab9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_
* * *
**LOCAL GOVERNMENT**
**" Former Mayor Mike Rawlings launches campaign to relocate Dallas City Hall, revive downtown"** via [Dallas News](https://substack.com/redirect/be9f4d3d-22ef-45f2-b17f-bb2c9bc2c00b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Devyani Chhetri** - **Mike Rawlings** is ramping up the fight over City Hall as questions grow over how to reshape downtown Dallas. Rawlings launched a coordinated campaign Thursday to build support for relocating City Hall, using newspaper and social media ads, a website and other outreach to promote redevelopment there, possibly for a sports arena and entertainment district.

In an interview with The Dallas Morning News, Rawlings said his efforts are designed to shift the City Council beyond wrangling over repair estimates and focus instead on how best to use the site as a catalyst to attract new business and reinvigorate its southern edge. "My fear about downtown is we're thinking too small," he said. "We've got to have a force to change this."

The campaign marks an escalation in the increasingly high-stakes fight over City Hall's future. It's been a clash of competing visions, centered on whether the council should invest in costly updates to the building or move government operations and pursue a different use for that large swath of land as the Dallas Mavericks look for a new home.

The council is expected to make that consequential choice in June after city staffers present a cost comparison of staying or leaving. Previous votes have indicated the mayor and eight council members support exploring relocation, while six members are opposed. _([DMN](https://substack.com/redirect/be9f4d3d-22ef-45f2-b17f-bb2c9bc2c00b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Mayor John Whitmire's new city budget shrinks Houston's future deficits"** via [Houston Chronicle](https://substack.com/redirect/8202cf30-c7ad-4048-9328-ee783c6f2454?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Abby Church** - Finance projections at Houston City Hall show steps city officials took to close a budget deficit in the proposal Mayor John Whitmire announced Tuesday would significantly reduce future red ink.

Whitmire's proposed $7.5 billion budget includes a new $5 monthly fee on city trash customers to help the city's troubled Solid Waste Management Department, which has long struggled to pick up trash, recycling and yard waste on time. That fee would generate $24 million in new revenue -- a rare step at City Hall.

But the proposal would also change the structure of the city budget by moving the $117 million solid waste budget out of the strained general fund and into Houston Public Works, within the city utility system.

The mayor also proposes charging the utility system $104 million - or 5% of its annual gross revenues - for its pipes using the city right of way, money that also would flow into the general fund. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/8202cf30-c7ad-4048-9328-ee783c6f2454?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Corpus Christi City Council votes to start talks on building a new desalination plant"** via [Spectrum News](https://substack.com/redirect/d1f707de-c82e-428c-b3e7-9130cb98bd95?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) -- As Corpus Christi's water crisis looms and city leaders scramble for solutions, the City Council has voted 6-2 to move forward with talks for a new company to build a desalination plant.

Houston-based AXE H2O is a two-month old company that says it can build a plant that can produce 150 million gallons of drinking water per day using natural gas, according to a report from The Texas Tribune. The city would pay $6.50 for 1,000 gallons of water.

According to **John Olson** , the company's chairman, the project would be a private venture and construction would take about two years. The company estimates it would cost about $1.3 billion to build.

Council members **Roland Barrera** and **Cynthia Campos** -- who made up the two votes against the project -- were skeptical, with Campos saying it sounded "too good to be true." _([Spectrum News](https://substack.com/redirect/d1f707de-c82e-428c-b3e7-9130cb98bd95?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" FBI says 6th Street shooter acted alone in March 1 mass shooting"** via [KXAN Austin](https://substack.com/redirect/7b04bf25-0a34-4f18-a6ee-66a44db4d4ef?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s Dalton Huey - The FBI said Thursday that its investigation into the March 1 mass shooting in downtown Austin found no evidence that the gunman was directed by a foreign terrorist organization. The press release notes that investigators learned that the perpetrator, **Ndiaga Diagne** , had expressed admiration for former Iranian Ayatollah**Ali Khamenei** and held grievances over American and Israeli attacks against Iran.

The FBI also stated that Diagne, a 53-year-old Senegal-born man and naturalized U.S. citizen as of 2013, had legally purchased a handgun in August 2017 and a rifle in October 2017. Diagne used both of those guns in his attack on West Sixth Street, in which he killed three people and injured 15 others. Responding Austin police officers confronted and killed him minutes after he opened fire.

The three killed in the shooting were **Savitha Shan** , **Ryder Harrington** and **Jorge Pederson**. In the initial aftermath of the attack, FBI officials said that there were "indicators" that it was an act of terrorism. The FBI said Thursday that its investigation determined Diagne acted alone and had not received outside funding, operational support or direction for the attack.

He also had not been the subject of any prior FBI investigation, according to the press release. Investigators also said Diagne's "violent behavior" escalated due to "specific personal triggers and grievances" connected to the Iran war. The FBI found Diagne admired Khamenei, who had been killed in the U.S. and Israeli attacks one day before the shooting. _([KXAN](https://substack.com/redirect/7b04bf25-0a34-4f18-a6ee-66a44db4d4ef?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

Ward** - Channelview-area leaders celebrated Wednesday after the Environmental Protection Agency ordered Waste Management and International Paper Co. to begin hauling toxic mud from a dioxin-filled waste pit that lurked in the San Jacinto River for decades.

"It's a good day to be in Harris County," said **Tom Ramsey** , the county commissioner for the area surrounding the waste pits, as he called the San Jacinto River the "lifeblood" of the region.

The cost estimate for cleanup of the underwater waste, known as the northern impoundment of the San Jacinto waste pits, has now climbed to a quarter of a billion dollars.

The companies do not have a mandated excavation date yet, though they must respond to the federal government within 10 days of the April 28 order. According to federal Superfund law, they could owe three times the total cost of work if the EPA has to take over cleanup efforts. _([HOU CHRON](https://substack.com/redirect/0e3df791-2b39-475b-b5cc-366e086cc758?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**BUSINESS NEWS**
**" BlackRock invests $30M in Texas electrician training amidst data center boom"** via [KXAN Austin](https://substack.com/redirect/82ef8eea-b0ac-4316-839e-507d382a3858?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s**Adam Schwager** -- Custom homebuilder **Gene Lantrip** has a slight problem. He's got a backload of about 15 houses right now, partially due to a recent boom of data centers in the region. "Oracle came in", he recalled "The next thing you know, they put out a call for 500 electricians"; Among those electricians were ones who helped put the finishing touches on the homes Lantrip builds.

"Local guys right now in Abilene, starting out and make $15 an hour, the good ones make up for $25 an hour," Lantrip says. He says the data center companies are willing to pay double -- and he can't compete. "So our electricians, what they started doing was hiring inexperienced young kids and teaching them the trades -- on-the-job training," he said. "My electrician used to have a team of about 12 guys... Now they have one lead guy and about five young kids... When they had 12 guys, they can knock out three houses, but now it takes them all day to do one house."

This comes at a time where the demand for Lantrip's services are as high as ever. "There's like 14,000 temporary workers out there working in right now, and they all need a place to stay," he said.

BlackRock, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, faces similar problems. "As the largest investor in infrastructure, we hear in every project, 'We don't have enough workers. We can't find the workers. We're challenged. We're going to have delays," BlackRock CEO **Larry Fink** said. "When you have delays in your projects, that means it costs more money." _([KXAN](https://substack.com/redirect/82ef8eea-b0ac-4316-839e-507d382a3858?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Nvidia could bring thousands of jobs to Austin. Here's how."** via [Austin American-Statesman](https://substack.com/redirect/6d0fbdf6-d868-4cc2-a800-1e6fbb1dbedb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Karoline Leonard** - Nvidia CEO **Jensen Huang** speaks with a Disney robot during an Nvidia conference focusing on artificial intelligence in San Jose, Calif., on March 16. The artificial intelligence chipmaker announced a partnership with glassmaker Corning to build three new factories in North Carolina and Texas, creating more than 3,000 new jobs.

The world's most valuable company might bring thousands of jobs to Austin as Nvidia ups its investment in Texas.

Artificial intelligence chipmaker Nvidia Corp. and glassmaker Corning Inc. announced plans to build three new plants dedicated to manufacturing light and glass technologies for AI manufacturing in North Carolina and Texas.

The companies, which both have significant business ties to the Austin area, promised to create more than 3,000 jobs at the factories. _([AAS](https://substack.com/redirect/6d0fbdf6-d868-4cc2-a800-1e6fbb1dbedb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

**" Is Brownsville getting a refinery? America First CEO is confident; industry analyst skeptical"** via [MyRGV.com](https://substack.com/redirect/3c0f4bc6-16e7-43f1-93e9-c68658c208a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)'s **Steve Clark** - When **Donald Trump** announced on Truth Social March 10 that Brownsville would be the site of the first U.S. oil refinery to be built in 50 years, it seemed to come out of the blue.

But in fact, Port of Brownsville officials have been in communication with the principals behind the proposed America First Refining (AFR) project for about a dozen years, according to Brownsville Navigation District Chairman **Steve Guerra**.

Back in June 2024, AFR founder and CEO **John Calce** announced that his company (then Element Fuel Holdings) had completed the site preparation and pre-construction work for a large oil refinery at the port. In a statement, he said the company had secured the permits necessary to construct and operate a refinery with a capacity of more than 160,000 BPD, or "approximately 6.7 million gallons, per day of finished gasoline, diesel and jet fuel."

Reuters reported at the time that Calce had tried before to build a refinery at the port, through start-up firms ARX Energy and Jupiter Brownsville LLC, one such attempt resulting in a bankruptcy filing. _([MY RGV](https://substack.com/redirect/3c0f4bc6-16e7-43f1-93e9-c68658c208a9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg))_

TOP NEWS " Heat stroke is suspected among 6 found dead in a shipping container at a rail yard near Texas border" via AP - A South Texas medical examiner believes heat stroke may have led to the death of six people thought to be immigrants who were found Sunday afternoon inside a shipping container at a Union Pacific rail yard near the Mexico border in Laredo, Texas. The people were found Sunday as workers were inspecting one of the containers, said Jose Baeza, a spokesperson for the Laredo Police Department. Police and fire crews arrived at the scene shortly afterward. They confirmed that there were six people dead, five men and one woman, Baeza told reporters. Dr. Corinne Stern , the Webb County Medical Examiner, is conducting autopsies and completed one for a 29-year-old Mexican woman who died of hyperthermia, or heat stroke. "I've ruled that an accidental death," she said. "I believe that the remaining individuals probably all succumbed to heat stroke as well, but their exams are not completed at this time, so I will not rule on their cause and manner yet." Stern found identification cards and cellphones that indicate the deceased may be from Mexico and Honduras, but fingerprints were taken and shared with U.S. Border Patrol to help confirm their identities and nationalities through the Missing Alien Program. The medical examiner's office also contacted the Mexican consulate after identifying the woman. "This was a horrific scene," Stern added, also noting that immigrant deaths is a common occurrence in the ten-county region her office covers. "This spring has been busier than it was this time last year," the medical examiner said. () " In parched Texas, a state fund to boost water projects falls almost $3 billion short of demand" via Colleen DeGuzman - As Texas struggles to meet the needs of a rapidly growing population, a state fund had $1.28 billion available this year to support projects that could deliver water even in a severe drought. Unfortunately, 23 worthy projects requested a total of $4.2 billion, prompting the state to deny 13 of them -- the first time the SWIFT fund had to say no to an applicant in its 11-year history. It was lamentable timing for a state plagued by a brutal drought and aging water infrastructure. "We have more demand than we actually have the capacity to fulfill this year," said Marvin Cole-Chaney , director of program administration and reporting for the Texas Water Development Board, which administers SWIFT, the State Water Implementation Fund for Texas. () " Gas power leapfrogs wind for first time in 10 years in Texas' grid connection queue" via Brandon Mulder and Chris Essig - A decade ago, wind power was surging in popularity and attracting huge investments that made Texas a national leader in renewable energy. But today, gas generation is making a big comeback, driven by a wave of data centers flooding into the state. For the last six months, the volume of gas generation in the Texas grid's interconnection queue -- the yearslong waiting list for electric generators wanting to connect to the grid -- has surpassed wind. It's the first time since January 2016 that gas has overtaken wind in the queue, a shift that reflects the policy and economic headwinds facing the wind industry and data centers favoring gas power as they seek to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom. "The data center explosion and their desire for 24/7 power probably excited a lot of gas developers, and that gas queue got bigger," said University of Texas professor of energy regulation David Spence. Like every power grid operator in the U.S., the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, or ERCOT, uses the interconnection queue to manage and plan for new power generation coming online. But not all projects in the queue ultimately reach completion. According to the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, or LBNL, only 22% of projects in ERCOT's queue actually get built, which is still the highest percentage of any grid in the nation. () " New Texas A&M president confirmed as university seeks stability" via AP - Regents on Wednesday unanimously appointed Susan Ballabina as president of Texas A&M, putting her in charge of the state's largest public university as it continues to deal with the fallout from its last president's resignation. Ballabina, who assumes the role on May 11, most recently served as executive vice chancellor for the Texas A&M University System, overseeing day-to-day operations across its 12 universities and eight state agencies. Prior to that, she was former Texas A&M President Mark A. Welsh III's chief of staff. Regents named Ballabina the sole finalist April 13. State law required them to wait 21 days before finalizing the hire. She initially served on the presidential search committee before recusing herself to apply for the job. "I was a reluctant applicant. I wasn't sure that this was something I wanted to do, but after going through the process and preparing for the various interviews, I got more and more excited," Ballabina said during the regents' meeting after their vote. The decision follows months of upheaval at the flagship campus after Welsh resigned amid political backlash over that was posted online. The search unfolded as regents took a more assertive role in responding to controversy and shaping what can be taught, part of a broader political remaking of Texas colleges under new state laws. () 2026 " Abbott's senior adviser warns Republicans not to let Texas flip" via Rachel Royster -** A senior adviser to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott warned two Tarrant County Republican clubs Wednesday of the possibility of Texas flipping if the party doesn't act. The same goes for Tarrant County, said Abbott's adviser and policy director, Steve Munisteri. Munisteri spoke to Tarrant Star Republican Women over lunch and the Cowtown Republican Women on Wednesday evening to discuss Texas' political landscape and what's at stake for Republicans () " How billionaires are helping Democrat James Talarico in the U.S. Senate race" via C. Moritz - James Talarico , a Texas Democratic primary candidate for U.S. Senate, frequently criticizes the influence of billionaires in politics and notably does not accept money from corporate political action committees. However, this does not preclude PACs and billionaires from promoting his campaign. Lone Star Rising, a super PAC created to support Talarico, has raised approximately $9 million from politically active billionaires and millionaires, with nearly half sourced from a dark money group that does not disclose its donors. Talarico has expressed support for banning super PACs and distances himself from Lone Star Rising, noting that federal law prohibits him from coordinating with the PAC or controlling its fundraising and spending. "Legally, I cannot do anything about what any super PAC does, whether supporting me or not supporting me," Talarico told reporters. "We've got super PACs on all sides. We've got super PACs in the middle that are playing on both sides. It's nothing that we have control over." () STATE GOVERNMENT " Texas reaches deal with youth camps over fiber‐optic rule tied to safety law" via Jack Fink - The Texas Department of State Health Services has struck a deal with youth camps over a requirement that they install a fiber‐optic internet connection to operate this summer. A group of camps filed suit against the state last month after the mandate was included in a camp safety law approved by lawmakers last year. The agreement stays the court proceedings until March 1, 2027. The legislation followed horrific flooding in Central Texas on July 4 that resulted in 25 campers and two counselors losing their lives at Camp Mystic. The camp's executive director also died. Under the agreement, camps that maintain redundant internet service and comply with all other safety requirements will not have their licenses denied if they have not installed fiber‐optic service. The agency said alternative broadband options - including cellular, microwave, or satellite - are acceptable as long as they meet the definition of broadband under the Texas Government Code. On Tuesday, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick and House Speaker Dustin Burrows , R‐Lubbock, issued a joint statement aimed at giving camps more flexibility. They acknowledged that some camps were struggling to comply and that other forms of reliable redundant internet access exist. () " Texas prisons saw 2,500% increase in overdose deaths in 7 years, TDCJ leader says" via Toluwani Osibamowo - Overdose deaths in Texas prisons jumped 2,480% over the past seven years, a state prison official told lawmakers this week as they consider ways to curb contraband in Texas correctional facilities. There were 129 recorded overdose deaths among people in Texas Department of Criminal Justice custody last year, said Bobby Lumpkin , TDCJ's executive director. That's up from five such deaths in 2018. The data was presented to senators Monday but has not been made publicly available online. It represents a relatively small portion of the 142,000 people Lumpkin said are currently in TDCJ custody. "The root cause is a dependency and an addiction to that type of illicit substances," he told lawmakers during a Senate Committee on Criminal Justice hearing. "It unfortunately is an extension of the criminal element that even though they've been through the judicial system, been sentenced, they still depend back on that type of activity." () " TEA selects Connally schools superintendent to lead takeover" via Sneha Dey - In a takeover of Connally ISD, the state brought in an educator from a neighboring Waco district to accelerate academic gains. Texas Education Agency Commissioner Mike Morath picked Josie Gutierrez to lead the 2,000-student district, citing her success in improving outcomes and strengthening teacher retention as deputy superintendent and an assistant superintendent of human resources for Waco ISD. Gutierrez is the latest superintendent Morath has appointed in recent weeks to helm districts after the commissioner took control from locally elected school trustees over poor academic performance. Other state interventions include those in Fort Worth, Lake Worth and Beaumont. () " AG Ken Paxton leaves Odessa hanging after tax investigation" via Carlos Nogueras Ramos - Last October was like any other for most Odessa city employees. Parks employees unveiled a new sign. The police department gave a tour to homeschooled kids. A council member attended a fundraising event for culinary students. But amid everyday responsibilities, top local officials were scrambling to respond to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton 's demand that they justify a recently approved tax rate hike. The state had just passed a law that prohibited cities from raising taxes without completing financial audits. Paxton had singled out four cities, and Odessa was among them. "To uphold my duty as the Attorney General to ensure that municipalities are following audit laws, I am formally launching an investigation into the City of Odessa to determine whether the new tax rate is illegal," Paxton wrote. "Furthermore, I am demanding that the new tax rate not be implemented until I complete my investigation." City officials moved quickly, gathering hundreds of pages of documents, including minutes from relevant City Council meetings and evidence that the tax rate was published in a newspaper. By December 2025, Odessa had handed over the documents Paxton requested. () LOCAL GOVERNMENT " Former Mayor Mike Rawlings launches campaign to relocate Dallas City Hall, revive downtown" via Devyani Chhetri - Mike Rawlings is ramping up the fight over City Hall as questions grow over how to reshape downtown Dallas. Rawlings launched a coordinated campaign Thursday to build support for relocating City Hall, using newspaper and social media ads, a website and other outreach to promote redevelopment there, possibly for a sports arena and entertainment district. In an interview with The Dallas Morning News, Rawlings said his efforts are designed to shift the City Council beyond wrangling over repair estimates and focus instead on how best to use the site as a catalyst to attract new business and reinvigorate its southern edge. "My fear about downtown is we're thinking too small," he said. "We've got to have a force to change this." The campaign marks an escalation in the increasingly high-stakes fight over City Hall's future. It's been a clash of competing visions, centered on whether the council should invest in costly updates to the building or move government operations and pursue a different use for that large swath of land as the Dallas Mavericks look for a new home. The council is expected to make that consequential choice in June after city staffers present a cost comparison of staying or leaving. Previous votes have indicated the mayor and eight council members support exploring relocation, while six members are opposed. () " Mayor John Whitmire's new city budget shrinks Houston's future deficits" via Church - Finance projections at Houston City Hall show steps city officials took to close a budget deficit in the proposal Mayor John Whitmire announced Tuesday would significantly reduce future red ink. Whitmire's proposed $7.5 billion budget includes a new $5 monthly fee on city trash customers to help the city's troubled Solid Waste Management Department, which has long struggled to pick up trash, recycling and yard waste on time. That fee would generate $24 million in new revenue -- a rare step at City Hall. But the proposal would also change the structure of the city budget by moving the $117 million solid waste budget out of the strained general fund and into Houston Public Works, within the city utility system. The mayor also proposes charging the utility system $104 million - or 5% of its annual gross revenues - for its pipes using the city right of way, money that also would flow into the general fund. () " Corpus Christi City Council votes to start talks on building a new desalination plant" via -- As Corpus Christi's water crisis looms and city leaders scramble for solutions, the City Council has voted 6-2 to move forward with talks for a new company to build a desalination plant. Houston-based AXE H2O is a two-month old company that says it can build a plant that can produce 150 million gallons of drinking water per day using natural gas, according to a report from The Texas Tribune. The city would pay $6.50 for 1,000 gallons of water. According to John Olson , the company's chairman, the project would be a private venture and construction would take about two years. The company estimates it would cost about $1.3 billion to build. Council members Roland Barrera and Cynthia Campos -- who made up the two votes against the project -- were skeptical, with Campos saying it sounded "too good to be true." () " FBI says 6th Street shooter acted alone in March 1 mass shooting" via Dalton Huey - The FBI said Thursday that its investigation into the March 1 mass shooting in downtown Austin found no evidence that the gunman was directed by a foreign terrorist organization. The press release notes that investigators learned that the perpetrator, Ndiaga Diagne , had expressed admiration for former Iranian AyatollahAli Khamenei and held grievances over American and Israeli attacks against Iran. The FBI also stated that Diagne, a 53-year-old Senegal-born man and naturalized U.S. citizen as of 2013, had legally purchased a handgun in August 2017 and a rifle in October 2017. Diagne used both of those guns in his attack on West Sixth Street, in which he killed three people and injured 15 others. Responding Austin police officers confronted and killed him minutes after he opened fire. The three killed in the shooting were Savitha Shan , Ryder Harrington and Jorge Pederson. In the initial aftermath of the attack, FBI officials said that there were "indicators" that it was an act of terrorism. The FBI said Thursday that its investigation determined Diagne acted alone and had not received outside funding, operational support or direction for the attack. He also had not been the subject of any prior FBI investigation, according to the press release. Investigators also said Diagne's "violent behavior" escalated due to "specific personal triggers and grievances" connected to the Iran war. The FBI found Diagne admired Khamenei, who had been killed in the U.S. and Israeli attacks one day before the shooting. () TRUMP ADMINISTRATION " EPA orders cleanup of toxic waste superfund site in San Jacinto River" via Rebekah F. Ward - Channelview-area leaders celebrated Wednesday after the Environmental Protection Agency ordered Waste Management and International Paper Co. to begin hauling toxic mud from a dioxin-filled waste pit that lurked in the San Jacinto River for decades. "It's a good day to be in Harris County," said Tom Ramsey , the county commissioner for the area surrounding the waste pits, as he called the San Jacinto River the "lifeblood" of the region. The cost estimate for cleanup of the underwater waste, known as the northern impoundment of the San Jacinto waste pits, has now climbed to a quarter of a billion dollars. The companies do not have a mandated excavation date yet, though they must respond to the federal government within 10 days of the April 28 order. According to federal Superfund law, they could owe three times the total cost of work if the EPA has to take over cleanup efforts. () BUSINESS NEWS " BlackRock invests $30M in Texas electrician training amidst data center boom" via Schwager -- Custom homebuilder Gene Lantrip has a slight problem. He's got a backload of about 15 houses right now, partially due to a recent boom of data centers in the region. "Oracle came in", he recalled "The next thing you know, they put out a call for 500 electricians"; Among those electricians were ones who helped put the finishing touches on the homes Lantrip builds. "Local guys right now in Abilene, starting out and make $15 an hour, the good ones make up for $25 an hour," Lantrip says. He says the data center companies are willing to pay double -- and he can't compete. "So our electricians, what they started doing was hiring inexperienced young kids and teaching them the trades -- on-the-job training," he said. "My electrician used to have a team of about 12 guys... Now they have one lead guy and about five young kids... When they had 12 guys, they can knock out three houses, but now it takes them all day to do one house." This comes at a time where the demand for Lantrip's services are as high as ever. "There's like 14,000 temporary workers out there working in right now, and they all need a place to stay," he said. BlackRock, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, faces similar problems. "As the largest investor in infrastructure, we hear in every project, 'We don't have enough workers. We can't find the workers. We're challenged. We're going to have delays," BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said. "When you have delays in your projects, that means it costs more money." () " Nvidia could bring thousands of jobs to Austin. Here's how." via Karoline Leonard - Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with a Disney robot during an Nvidia conference focusing on artificial intelligence in San Jose, Calif., on March 16. The artificial intelligence chipmaker announced a partnership with glassmaker Corning to build three new factories in North Carolina and Texas, creating more than 3,000 new jobs. The world's most valuable company might bring thousands of jobs to Austin as Nvidia ups its investment in Texas. Artificial intelligence chipmaker Nvidia Corp. and glassmaker Corning Inc. announced plans to build three new plants dedicated to manufacturing light and glass technologies for AI manufacturing in North Carolina and Texas. The companies, which both have significant business ties to the Austin area, promised to create more than 3,000 jobs at the factories. () " Is Brownsville getting a refinery? America First CEO is confident; industry analyst skeptical" via Steve Clark - When Donald Trump announced on Truth Social March 10 that Brownsville would be the site of the first U.S. oil refinery to be built in 50 years, it seemed to come out of the blue. But in fact, Port of Brownsville officials have been in communication with the principals behind the proposed America First Refining (AFR) project for about a dozen years, according to Brownsville Navigation District Chairman Steve Guerra. Back in June 2024, AFR founder and CEO John Calce announced that his company (then Element Fuel Holdings) had completed the site preparation and pre-construction work for a large oil refinery at the port. In a statement, he said the company had secured the permits necessary to construct and operate a refinery with a capacity of more than 160,000 BPD, or "approximately 6.7 million gallons, per day of finished gasoline, diesel and jet fuel." Reuters reported at the time that Calce had tried before to build a refinery at the port, through start-up firms ARX Energy and Jupiter Brownsville LLC, one such attempt resulting in a bankruptcy filing. Why is the DCCC backing a conservative Dem over Randy Villegas?
# [](https://act.leaderswedeserve.com/go/852?refcode=em20260511-1&t=1&akid=3466%2E587540%2E29zFFW)
Peter -- another day, another reason to be pissed off at the Dem establishment.
**Right now, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is putting its thumb on the scale to back a conservative Democrat over progressive candidate (and LWD endorsee) Randy Villegas.**
Establishment Democrats claim to want a big tent party -- until it starts to include real progressive fighters who don’t answer to corporations, billionaires, or big pharma.

And yet, the DCCC is ignoring Randy’s momentum in order to back the candidate who:
* was the only Democrat to vote with Republicans against Prop 50
* shares nearly 60 corporate donors with the Republican incumbent
* couldn’t even show up to a vote forcing ICE agents to remove their masks

Ending Sexual Assault in the Military

# [Bangor Hands Out $336k in Grants to "Food and Medicine" That Employed Troy Jackson And Campaigned for Liberal City Councilors](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2246936&post_id=197231322&utm_source=post-email-title&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MTk3MjMxMzIyLCJpYXQiOjE3Nzg1MzcyMTYsImV4cCI6MTc4MTEyOTIxNiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTIyNDY5MzYiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.WUbEdmBtzIUGgCZJVNODNc_XDJovK9lntN7me-mWtuM)
